body: As three siblings came of age and had to leave their pack, scientists tracked the dogs’ perilous 2,500-mile odyssey to find their own territory It sounds like a Disney movie: three wild dogs, all brothers, on an epic journey to find a home of their own after their family tells them to leave
They dodge cars and hunters in search of a new life, navigating bushmeat snares and the hostility of a human-dominated landscape until they find a new haven on the African savannah
But this is exactly what happened in Zambia last year, when three endangered African wild dogs made the longest-ever recorded single journey of any mammal from the continent

The brothers travelled more than 2,500 miles (4,100km) over eight months in their “dispersal” – when a young dog comes of age and must establish new territory to find a mate and start a family of their own

title: Pay No Attention to the Russian Oligarch at My Wedding Weekend
excerpt: Welcome to our wedding weekend! It’s going to be a beautiful occasion, followed by an intimate gathering of family, dear friends, and one Russian oligarch nobod
body: Welcome to our wedding weekend! It’s going to be a beautiful occasion, followed by an intimate gathering of family, dear friends, and one Russian oligarch nobody knows who will be handed the bill afterward
The bride will wear white, the groom will wear white, and the Russian oligarch nobody knows will wear camouflage in case someone tries to take a picture of him and ProPublica finds out
We will try to pass him off as a tropical plant, or suggest that he was doing close-up magic
That whole celebration was magic! To be clear, there is no ethical concern involving the Russian oligarch (part of Vladimir Putin’s recent delegation to China) sponsoring this lavish event
This was not actually a wedding after-party; it was a fun weekend that had been planned long in advance of the wedding, which our guests also happened to attend right after we got married

Totally different! To those who say, “I still don’t know if a friend of Putin should be paying for this,” we say, “Who can truly say who is friends with another person?” This man paid hundreds of thousands of dollars for our three-day post-wedding celebration, but Eric Trump says he has “absolutely no clue who this person is,” nor has he ever heard his name
A dear friend? A total stranger? Doesn’t matter
The Supreme Court says money is speech , and we’ve taken that to heart

Fifty dollars means “Hello.” Five hundred thousand dollars means “I want to hang out with Donald Trump Jr. in an unmarked Georgetown basement.” Footing most of the bill for a three-day island extravaganza is just “Congratulations to the happy couple!” To those worried that the president might owe special favors to people present for his offspring’s wedding day, relax! This is not like The Godfather
In The Godfather , his daughter was getting married
The president doesn’t have to grant any favors you ask on his son’s wedding day
In fact, it’s bad luck to ask for favors at a son’s wedding! Let alone his second one
Also, the attorney general, Todd Blanche, says there’s nothing sketchy here to investigate
Everyone knows that it is only corruption when it comes from the Biden family
Anyways, having an oligarch of unclear provenance at your most intimate celebrations (sorry, the after-party for your most intimate celebrations) is a very normal thing, we think

These are the little details that make every wedding: the bridesmaids, getting their hair and makeup done; the best man, rushing to finish his toast; and the oligarch, handing over fistfuls of unmarked bills to all of the entertainers

Every American can relate to this! Remember Ross’s wedding on Friends , when Monica and Chandler couldn’t find Ross’s oligarch, and everybody thought the wedding couldn’t go forward? Remember the morning of your own wedding, when you were scrambling to make sure you had something borrowed, something blue, and somebody’s oligarch paying for you? (The oligarch has nothing to do with something borrowed, because that implies we’ll be paying him back somehow; this is just a gift from the kindness of his heart.) You may be wondering what to bring us! No gifts, please

title: ‘The Best Thing That Happened to Him Was Losing in 2020’
excerpt: Few reporters understand as much about Donald Trump’s thinking, motives, and behavior as Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan
body: Few reporters understand as much about Donald Trump’s thinking, motives, and behavior as Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan

Haberman has been covering the president closely for more than a decade at The New York Times ; she started with his first campaign in 2015, and her record of scoops quickly brought her into the public eye
Swan was, for many years, her chief professional rival: He worked for Axios , where he landed a controversial 2018 one-on-one interview with Trump
In late 2022, the Times announced that it was hiring Swan, turning the rivals into colleagues
This past June, they published Regime Change: Inside the Imperial Presidency of Donald Trump

The book, an instant best seller, advances a new understanding of the first year of Trump’s second term, relaying in minute-by-minute detail how, since retaking office, he has pursued his personal goals with few limits on his power
The Atlantic staff writer Tim Alberta sat down with both authors at The Atlantic Festival, where he asked them about the 2028 election and the future of the presidency and the Republican Party
This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity
Tim Alberta: Maggie, this country has been through a lot, and I’m wondering if you could help us understand how a “regime change” of this sort came to be
Maggie Haberman: Essentially, we have had a series of national traumas since 9/11: two forever wars, a fiscal crisis, immense populist anger that started rising in 2010
To me, that was the year that set the tone
It was also the year that the proto-Trump, Carl Paladino, was the Republican nominee for governor in New York State

One of the issues that he ran on was the planned mosque to be built near the World Trade Center; it became known incorrectly as the “Ground Zero Mosque,” and it became a clear avatar of a change in this country after the era of George W
So you get to 2014, when immigration and particularly border crossings were on the rise under President Obama
Suddenly, this became a massive issue within the Republican Party
You had this mix of anger over the wars, anger over the massive accumulated debt under President Bush, then Obamacare, anger about immigration, and a shifting job market
The time was ripe for a candidate who presented himself as a fighter—and who was already known to most of the Republican electorate, not just as a celebrity on The Apprentice but as a cultural figure
Alberta: 2016, Trump 1.0, is its own story

So much of what this book is about is how the end of that first term, and then his time in exile after losing in 2020, shapes this dramatic, radical, wholesale change to government and to executive power

Jonathan Swan: When we were reporting for this book, we heard from a couple of people who were close to Trump at a pretty high level that, in their view, the best thing that happened to him was losing in 2020
Which is something they could never say publicly or in his presence, because, of course, he never lost the election and what have you
Let’s say Trump ekes out that victory in 2020: He comes back in; he is hobbled by COVID
He has the same inflation that every other country around the world has
He still has the rump of a team around him that he really doesn’t like very much, who are, in quite a few instances, pushing back on some of his more extreme desires
He really can’t get his arms around the presidency
People like Stephen Miller spent those four years very productively
It wasn’t just drawing up the plans—you saw that blitz of executive orders at the start of 2025, which was all very well prepared

They also spent a lot of time thinking about Who are the lawyers that we want to fill the government with? And I’m not just talking about the White House counsel’s office; I’m talking about across the government
Agency lawyers, general counsels—they would constantly say, Well, no, what you’re proposing is illegal
But when you have lawyers who are saying, Well, actually, if we turn it this way and then turn it this way and then give it a little bit of a spin , then they can bless what you want

I’ll give you the perfect example that describes the difference between term one and term two: In term one, Trump was saying almost yearningly, You know, they don’t have a drug problem in China, because Xi Jinping, he just kills the drug dealers
And they don’t have a drug problem in the Philippines, because Rodrigo Duterte just kills them
Trump was very fond of these extrajudicial killings
In term one, there wasn’t a huge amount of enthusiasm for this idea among the leadership of the Defense Department

Now you have Pete Hegseth, and you have lawyers inside the government that allow a policy where Donald Trump decided, in his mind, that people on fishing boats transporting cocaine in the Caribbean Sea are not drug traffickers who are to be interdicted by the Coast Guard and dealt with in a criminal-justice system
And that’s something that has been blessed within the government
They haven’t even bothered to try to legally justify this in a public setting

They just do it, knowing that they have the right lawyers in place. [ Read: Pete Hegseth delights in violence ] The other big element making this term unrecognizable from the first term is the immunity decision
Maggie and I talk about this all the time
Trump would say early on, I’m immune; I’m immune

title: When Meditation Has a Dark Side
excerpt: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Overcast | Pocket Casts Twenty years ago, a meditation teacher and doctoral candidate in clinical psycholog
body: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Overcast | Pocket Casts Twenty years ago, a meditation teacher and doctoral candidate in clinical psychology named Willoughby Britton set out to do a study showing that meditation improves sleep

She divided up the participants, sent them to a sleep lab to monitor their brain activity, and discovered that the results were the opposite of what she had hoped for: The more they meditated, the worse their quality of sleep got

Britton had already experienced benefits of meditation herself, which are well documented in medical literature: It soothes anxiety, chronic pain, and depression, and it lowers blood pressure, alleviates back pain, and has many other benefits, as well
But as she continued to look into it, Britton kept discovering what seemed, at first, like exceptions: people who actually became more anxious or unmotivated after meditating
Then she began encountering people who experienced more serious mental-health side effects, such as paranoia, hallucinations, and dissociation
Britton became a researcher at Brown University and eventually developed a robust body of work showing that meditation—for certain people and at certain intensities—can be harmful
On this episode of Radio Atlantic is the staff writer Olga Khazan, who interviewed Britton about her research
We talk about how the meditation community responded, how Britton’s life changed after it was released, and what her recommendations are for the average person interested in meditation
The following is a transcript of the episode: Hanna Rosin: Just a quick warning: This episode mentions suicide
If you or someone you know is in crisis, call or text the U.S
National Suicide Prevention Lifeline at 988. [ Music ] Rosin: This is Radio Atlantic
I was once at a yoga retreat where early-morning meditation was one of the things on the schedule
I woke up, sat down, and lasted about 12 minutes, which felt like 90
I downloaded the Calm app a couple of years ago, and I have used it exactly zero times
I have a doctor friend who assured me that meditation was one of a handful of nonmedicine treatments that had been thoroughly vetted by peer-reviewed science journals, so I never gave up trying
I just assumed that this was my fault and I needed to get better at it

I have definitely absorbed the idea that there is a meditation ideal to strive towards, a master of serene who manages to both embody a Western principle of high-stress job and an Eastern principle of no stress at all
Olga Khazan: So I don’t know exactly how it made the leap over from India to America
I think that happened in the 19th century
Khazan: But this modern moment of meditation that we’re living in started in Silicon Valley tech companies

So probably around 10 or 15 years ago, a lot of tech companies—I was gonna say cling , but you’re not really supposed to cling in meditation—they started glomming onto meditation as this solution for people being burned out and overworked
Arianna Huffington: There is a deeper dimension to our lives, and we can tap into it
Khazan: I think Oprah probably did it at one point
Oprah Winfrey: 9 o’clock in the morning, 4:30 in the afternoon, no matter what’s going on, we stop
Announcer 1: Look, LeBron meditating there on the bench
Announcer 2: He’s in that— Announcer 1: Becoming present
Khazan: Google had a meditation session for its employees

People in positions of power and authority and people who everyone thought was cool were kind of pushing this idea that meditation is this very benign sort of thing that you can do for yourself in order to make yourself more relaxed

And I would say that there was a subtext there of, And it’ll make you more productive because you won’t be so obsessed with, like, dumb bullshit . ( Laughs .) [ Music ] Rosin: Today, meditation is a multibillion-dollar industry
According to one study, about half of all Americans have tried meditation
She tried something called MBSR, or mindfulness-based stress reduction, although reluctantly
Khazan: This was one of the most annoying things about it for me, is that it was very loosey-goosey
But then whenever I asked if I could modify it in some way, it was like, No, that’s the wrong way to do it . ( Laughs .) Rosin: But Olga says it did help relieve some of her anxiety
Khazan: So even though I wasn’t very good at meditation, I did buy this idea that it’s basically harmless
It seems like, oh, the worst thing that could happen is it just doesn’t work, because you’re not good at it
Honestly, I’ve taken a whole meditation class, where I meditated for 45 minutes a day, and I don’t think anyone ever said, This could be risky
Rosin: That’s what I always thought, too, and why I at least liked the idea of meditation
It has a low barrier to entry—no fancy, expensive equipment or services required—and seemingly zero side effects
But then one day, as Olga was browsing online, she came across a researcher at Brown University named Willoughby Britton
Khazan: So Willoughby Britton started out as a very avid meditator, pretty much as avid as they get

title: College Is Coming Apart
excerpt: Sign up for Ordinary Extraordinary , Ian Bogost’s newsletter on making everyday life vivid
body: Sign up for Ordinary Extraordinary , Ian Bogost’s newsletter on making everyday life vivid
Artificial intelligence arrived on campus as a crisis but has since become banal
Students can now do basically all their schoolwork automatically with AI—answering scientific problem sets, writing computer code, and drafting essays
Professors like me have no idea whether we are really teaching or just LARPing for students who are also pretending to occupy their role
Worse, some of us are offloading the drudgery of writing recommendation letters , grant proposals , and even scientific papers to AI
But at the same time that AI fouled up the student-teacher relationship, the technology benefited other corners of campus

Researchers quickly discovered that AI is enormously useful for knowledge production, especially in the natural and applied sciences: in protein-structure prediction , materials design , and drug discovery , for example
Pressured, in part, by donors, boards, employers, and parents, college administrators have announced AI initiatives , invested in AI infrastructure , and established AI degree programs
These two forces—students using AI to their detriment and colleges using it to their benefit—might seem to be in conflict
Students are supposed to do everything longhand to preserve the sanctity of learning, but they are also urged to meet the new professional demands created by AI
Faculty and administrators are policing the classroom for AI, largely in vain, while also using AI liberally in their own work
Campuses are defending themselves against AI as an interloper while concurrently retooling themselves for the AI future
Colleges are racing toward and away from AI simultaneously
It feels like artificial intelligence is wresting higher education apart
But I’ve come to the conclusion that something bigger, stranger, and more damaging has been taking place for a long time

AI has combined with two other recent campus crises— the coronavirus pandemic and the research-funding cuts of the second Trump administration —to amplify a deeper truth: American college is incompatible with itself
Americans speak of “college” as if it is one coherent thing
Higher education is a bundle of unrelated things held together by custom, history, and accident
The college bundle was always a tenuous one
It has little reason to remain together, even as the institutions inside it are too entrenched to separate
On the one hand, college is a credentialing service: It awards a degree that affirms knowledge and sends a graduate into a career
On the other hand, college is a coming-of-age service
It forms identity through social exploration and intellectual development
It is the American ideal for how a young person figures out who they are
Partying, drinking, Greek life, sports, and other forms of college life always risked undermining the educational project—and vice versa
But the two categories coexisted well enough. [ Listen: Where do America’s colleges go from here? ] Now two things that got packaged together as “college” have begun to unbundle and disperse

The coming-of-age experience—friendships, independence, experimentation—has become less obviously dependent on the campus surrounding it, partly because college’s monopoly on exposure to a wider world weakened
Globalization and the internet bring much of that world to students long before they arrive on campus
Other aspects of college life have been moving off campus too
College football has gone national, abandoning regional affinities and local rivalries
Greek rush has become an outsourced industry
Campuses are hospital systems, major local employers, and real-estate-investment operations as much as, or more than, they are schools
Optimizing college for professional preparation also began to pull the two purposes apart, and eroded the unrepeatable social experience that college is supposed to provide
The economy demanded more of students outside the classroom —internships, networking, publications, volunteering

In a brutal job-search environment , where entry-level gigs seem to demand nepotism, luck, and 10 rounds of interviews, today’s undergraduates may feel that their older professors do not fully understand the gap between the delivery of the credential and the career it promises
Then COVID-19 revealed that the credentialing process could continue if campus life was reduced or even eliminated entirely
Considerable controversy and confusion accompanied this moment; some students tried to sue expensive universities on the grounds that a closed campus was not worth the full-freight price
But in the end, credentialing proved entirely possible with a compromised or absent version of campus life
Now AI has separated the two purposes of college almost entirely
Writing an essay previously required doing something resembling the assigned academic work

title: Why the Bomb Is Bad for Democracy
excerpt: “In August of 1945, the city of Hiroshima was destroyed in about nine seconds by a single atomic bomb.” So begins the 1981 documentary The Day After Trinity , i
body: “In August of 1945, the city of Hiroshima was destroyed in about nine seconds by a single atomic bomb.” So begins the 1981 documentary The Day After Trinity , in a voice-over against a black background. “The man responsible for building the bomb was a gentle and eloquent physicist named J
Robert Oppenheimer.” Directed by a young filmmaker named Jon Else and financed by a public-television station in San Jose, The Day After Trinity quickly became a hit across the United States
One of its innovations was to pair the story of the bomb with that of Oppenheimer, foregrounding the contradiction of this “gentle” pacifist giving the nation its greatest weapon of war
Hecht has argued , Else’s film helped transform Oppenheimer from a Cold War political figure into a symbol of the profound moral dilemmas inherent in the nuclear age
In the years since the documentary premiered, Americans have continued to view Oppenheimer (and, by extension, his bomb) through Else’s lens
American Prometheus , the Pulitzer Prize–winning biography written by Kai Bird and Martin J
Sherwin, repeatedly cites Else’s interview transcripts and largely replicates his approach
Oppenheimer , Christopher Nolan’s blockbuster 2023 film adaption of the book, does much the same
Now Else, at 82, has revisited the bomb, this time in a nonfiction book he’s been working on for 20 years

Yet Frenchman Flat: The Rise and Fall of Atomic Bombs is not another story of the doomed Oppenheimer; Else relies on his own remarkable interviews from almost half a century ago but doesn’t focus on the scientist, and he declines to “relitigate the decision to drop the bomb” on Japan

Neither is Frenchman Flat quite what its publisher is promoting, the “story of a single nuclear bomb” (a 37-kiloton nuke called Priscilla that exploded over Frenchman Flat , a dry lake bed in Nevada, in 1957)
That story, though compellingly told, disappears for whole swaths of the text

Instead, much to its credit, the book unspools an unhurried, capacious story of human society’s collective journey to the brink of annihilation, and of the individuals and movements that have, so far, held us back from the edge

It is a major work, highlighting the heroism and the absurdity of our atomic present and this Strangelovian, Lovecraftian thing we call “nuclear policy.” [ Read: The nuclear club might soon double ] Today, the famous Doomsday Clock , which measures the risk of nuclear cataclysm, is at just 85 seconds from midnight, the closest it’s been to Armageddon since the clock’s creation in 1947

After decades of disarmament, Russia, China, France, and several other nuclear powers are rapidly expanding their arsenals, while Germany, South Korea, Japan, and others are considering developing their own programs
The agreements that long ago halted U.S. and Russian testing recently expired
Donald Trump has been expressing an alarming interest in the use of nuclear weapons for decades
Among Else’s most important accomplishments is recognizing how crucial secrecy has been to the maintenance of nuclear stockpiles

Since the bomb was first developed, the U.S. government has denied the public basic facts about atomic weapons. “The extreme secrecy surrounding almost everything concerning nuclear weapons impeded effective democratic debate for decades,” one report quoted by Else concluded
The bomb, in other words, is bad for democracy, just as democracy is bad for the bomb
The tight grip on information goes back to the beginning—to the Manhattan Project , which brought hundreds of scientists and their families to the New Mexico desert to build an unprecedented weapon
At the height of World War II, the U.S. military concluded that the decision to develop a bomb could not be subject to public debate
Congress, the historian Alex Hellerstein has calculated , only about 1 percent were brought into the loop
In 1943, the wartime Office of Censorship banned media references to “war experiments,” and officials issued false or misleading responses to press inquiries

Thus, when a bomb exploded onto Hiroshima and “instantly broiled the skin of every person in the open within half a mile,” in Else’s appropriately gruesome phrasing, almost everyone on the planet was genuinely shocked
But that was wartime—and the cessation of hostilities generated new complexities
Could this degree of unaccountability really persist in a time of peace? Else’s interview subjects felt that it shouldn’t
Within weeks of Japan’s surrender, hundreds of Manhattan Project scientists put out a statement calling for “free and enlightened public discussion” of atomic power
Oppenheimer and liberal members of Harry S
Truman’s administration quickly proposed a plan to place control of all nuclear materials and weapons in the hands of the United Nations
As the historian Daniel Immerwahr has noted , much of the scientific community went so far as to seek a “global government” to regulate the bomb
Today this idea might seem unthinkable, but in the ’40s, the notion enjoyed the support of such wild-eyed radicals as Winston Churchill, Richard Nixon, John F
The postwar constitutions of France and Italy explicitly countenanced a future global body that would trump their own sovereignty
Else cites polls suggesting that about two-thirds of Americans supported some version of this concept. [ Read: What Trump doesn’t understand about nuclear war ] It did not come to pass
U.S. leaders waffled on the idea, and eventually the U.S.S.R., hastily developing a bomb of its own, rejected it

What, then, to do with America’s swelling nuclear arsenal? Many elected officials feared that some “dashing lieutenant colonel” might go rogue with a nuke or three, and so in 1946, Congress passed the Atomic Energy Act, taking control of the bomb away from the military and placing it solely in the hands of the president

Given the trigger-happy proposals floated by many within the military brass in the years to follow, this structure may well have saved countless lives, but it hardly provided for democratic accountability, much less actual arms control

The historian Garry Wills has powerfully argued that the postwar nuclear chain of command altered the United States “down to its deepest constitutional roots,” giving the president exclusive and unfettered power far beyond the comprehension of our country’s founders

Kennedy, for one, considered the presidential nuclear prerogative “insane.” Much of Frenchman Flat is devoted to documenting the insanity that resulted from a nuclear-powered state (and, soon, states) freed from checks and balances and uninterested in public debate
There was no public hearing concerning the U.S. decision to start exploding nuclear bombs in Nevada in 1951; the state’s governor heard about it only a week before the first bomb fell

Meet a mouse whose brain cortex is made up of human cells Multiple cameras tracked a mouse as it wandered around a small arena
A computer charted its position and speed, leaving Pong-like traces on a monitor
The reason to watch this rodent so carefully? Nearly half its brain volume had been replaced with human cells
A team at Stanford has revealed the effort to mix brain tissues of distant species this week
They previously showed that human brain organoids could survive, and even function, after being injected into the heads of baby rodents
Now, they’ve taken things a step further by genetically modifying mice so their brains don’t fully develop in the first place
The work could help scientists study brain injuries, but it also raises questions about how far these experiments should go

There are also efforts to make AI more energy-efficient, track pollution more effectively, and turn invasive weeds and food waste into useful materials

Get to know the innovators and their breakthroughs . —Casey Crownhart This story is from The Spark, our weekly climate tech newsletter

title: Meet the innovators under 35 shaping climate tech
excerpt: AI is reshaping climate tech, for better and worse
body: AI is reshaping climate tech, for better and worse
Young innovators are using machine learning to track pollution and build better city-scale climate models
There's also a need to help reduce AI's energy demand
The race for critical minerals is heating up

Lithium shortages could hit this decade, and two innovators are tackling the problem from opposite angles—one extracting lithium faster from brine, another making hardrock ore a cheaper, viable source
Climate solutions are hiding in unexpected places

From a furnace that simplifies steelmaking to bioplastics made from invasive weeds, there are surprising problems and solutions across all corners of the economy. " data-chronoton-post-id="1144251" data-chronoton-expand-collapse="1" data-chronoton-analytics-enabled="1"> Each year, the editorial team at MIT Technology Review puts together a list of 35 innovators under 35—a group of researchers, inventors, and other young minds worth following
The team worked on the newest edition of the list for months, and the final slate includes nine individuals from all over the world in the climate and energy category
Each one has a fascinating story and is tackling an important challenge
I think it’s worth zooming out and considering the energy and climate awardees as a group
Taken together, these innovators and their work can tell us something about where climate tech is at this moment—and where it’s heading
AI is the dominant technology story, both for its potential and its challenges
We split the innovators into four main categories this year: biotech, climate and energy, computing and robotics, and AI
It probably won’t surprise you that AI features heavily in the work of many innovators in other categories
Climate innovator Jae-Won Chung , for example, built software to make AI more energy-efficient

By measuring the energy demands of open-source models, he hopes the industry can better understand and address the impact of AI. (If this work sounds familiar, it’s because we spoke with him last year for our investigation into AI’s energy demands .) But AI also has the potential to improve many areas of research
Jing Wei is using AI to track pollution more effectively, essentially using machine learning to fill in gaps in data from disparate sources like satellites and weather stations
Zhonghua Zheng developed AI climate models that work better for cities, a well-known blind spot for traditional models
We need better ways to get the critical materials used to build new technologies
As we begin to rely on new technologies to power our world, we’ll see a major shift in the materials we need to build them
Lithium is a prime example: The metal underpins lithium-ion batteries, which are crucial not only for electric vehicles, but also for large-scale energy storage on the grid
We could face lithium shortages as soon as this decade, and the prospect of supply crunches applies to other critical minerals, too—copper is another one to watch closely
Brine is currently the cheapest source of lithium, but the process to get the metal out can take months and harm the local environment
Mohammad Alkhadra is the cofounder and CEO of Lithios, a startup working to quickly and efficiently extract lithium from brines
Hardrock ore is the most common source of lithium, but it’s more expensive than brine
Benjamin Mowbray cofounded and serves as CTO for Rock Zero, which is working to extract lithium from hardrock ore
Addressing climate change will require overhauling all corners of our society, sometimes in surprising ways
To reach net-zero greenhouse gas emissions we will obviously need to rethink major sectors, like the electrical grid and transportation, to move away from fossil fuels
But outside these primary sources of climate pollution are seemingly infinite, less obvious problems to figure out, too
Heavy industry, including steel production, is a major one, making up about 7% of global greenhouse gas emissions
Laureen Meroueh is making cleaner, cheaper steel using a new kind of furnace that simplifies the chemical process required to produce the metal
Plastics are generally made with fossil fuels, so we’ll need alternatives to this incredibly useful category of materials
Joseph Nguthiru is making a bioplastic replacement for fossil-derived packaging that uses an invasive weed
Also using available materials in a creative way, Diana Orembe is making fish food for aquaculture with food waste
And refrigerants are often incredibly powerful greenhouse gases
Jinyoung Seo is developing solid refrigerants that could eliminate worries about leakage
A device using these materials could reduce energy consumption by 20% compared to conventional technology
I’m constantly learning about new challenges we face in the climate and energy world, and I’m often surprised by the ideas people are coming up with to address them
For more on all the under-35 innovators and their work, check out our full 2026 list
This article is from The Spark, MIT Technology Review ’s weekly climate newsletter

title: La importancia de enseñar a los estudiantes lo que la IA no puede hacer

<title>La importancia de enseñar a los estudiantes lo que la IA no puede hacer</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760123/original/file-20260819-50-terihh.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C1720%2C3159%2C2106&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">«Madeleine en el Bois d&#39;Amour» (1888), de Émile Bernard.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/madeleine-in-the-bois-damour-1888-from-the-collection-of-news-photo/1151163973?adppopup=true">Art Media/The Print Collector via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Resulta inquietante imaginar que el pensamiento humano pueda volverse obsoleto o ser considerado inferior debido a los avances en inteligencia artificial. Pero, a pesar de todos sus problemas, la IA no puede ignorarse ni descartarse. Ha llegado para quedarse, y quiero que mis alumnos comprendan lo que está en juego si dependemos demasiado de esta tecnología.</p>

<p>No puedo culparlos por preguntarse por qué deberían dedicar tanto tiempo y esfuerzo a <a href="https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/blog/college-confidential/202508/why-human-writing-is-essential-in-the-age-of-ai">perfeccionar su escritura</a> y sus habilidades de pensamiento crítico si los grandes modelos de lenguaje parecen hacer un trabajo aceptable.</p>

<p>Sin embargo, esta situación tiene importantes implicaciones para la cultura y las sociedades. </p>

<p>Es fácil imaginar un futuro en el que la dependencia de la IA conduzca al conformismo intelectual y a la erosión del pensamiento crítico. Los investigadores <a href="https://theconversation.com/ai-induced-cultural-stagnation-is-no-longer-speculation-its-already-happening%20-272488">ya están documentando estos efectos</a>, que amenazan con convertir el <a href="https://www.forbes.com/sites/timbajarin/2026/07/21/the-quiet-death-of-critical-thinking-in-the-age-of-ai-summaries/">esfuerzo de lidiar con las ideas en un arte perdido</a>.</p>

<p>Por eso creo que es fundamental que los educadores enfrenten la IA de frente. La clave, en mi opinión, es enseñar a los estudiantes a distinguir <a href="https://pe.gatech.edu/blog/industry-trends/ai-and-data-science">las habilidades de reconocimiento de patrones de la IA</a> de su incapacidad para soñar despierta, ponerse en el lugar de los demás y expresarse de manera auténtica.</p>

<h2>Dime qué piensas</h2>

<p>En un curso que impartí recientemente sobre literatura gótica sureña, les propuse un ejercicio a mis alumnos. Se les pidió que le pidieran a la IA que analizara la «atmósfera emocional» de una escena de la novela de Carson McCullers de 1940, «<a href="https://www.harpercollins.com/products/heart-is-a-lonely-hunter-carson-mccullers?variant=39973876301858">El corazón es un cazador solitario</a>».</p>

<p>Muchos de los personajes que los lectores conocen en <a href="https://www.uncannymagazine.com/article/southern-gothic-shadows-superstition-and-the-supernatural/">las obras del gótico sureño</a>, como las de McCullers, son extravagantes y brutales. Retratados desde una perspectiva distorsionada y antinatural, hablan en dialectos extraños y evocan lo que <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/books/2025/mar/25/so-much-more-than-southern-gothic-flannery-oconnor-at-100">Flannery O’Connor</a> se refirió al «<a href="https://www.themarginalian.org/%2025/03/2014/flannery-o-connor-lectura-del-grotesco/">grotesco</a>.» </p>

<p>Viven en lugares aislados que parecen anclados en el pasado y que, por usar otra expresión de O’Connor, están «<a href="https://www.nightmare-magazine.com/nonfiction/the-h-word-the-dirty-south/">perseguidos por Cristo</a>». </p>

<p>A muchos lectores les cuesta asimilar los extraños mundos de estos personajes. A la IA le resulta aún más difícil generalizar las complejas tensiones entre la fe y la incredulidad, o entre el bien y el mal, que dan vida a estas historias.</p>

<figure class="align-right zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/754365/original/file-20260817-60-6elr37.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Foto en blanco y negro de una mujer joven sentada en el escalón de una entrada, con la cabeza apoyada en una mano y un cigarrillo entre los dedos de la otra." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/754365/original/file-20260817-60-6elr37.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=237&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/754365/original/file-20260817-60-6elr37.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=727&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/754365/original/file-20260817-60-6elr37.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=727&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/754365/original/file-20260817-60-6elr37.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=727&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/754365/original/file-20260817-60-6elr37.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=914&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/754365/original/file-20260817-60-6elr37.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=914&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/754365/original/file-20260817-60-6elr37.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=914&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Carson McCullers.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/Carson%20McCullers/c1f89f8c33814555ac3ca8e8e1bc8122/photo">AP Photo</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Para limitar el abanico de respuestas y permitir comparaciones útiles, les proporcioné a los estudiantes escenas en las que aparecían los personajes principales de la novela. Una de ellas era la secuencia desgarradora en la que Spiros Antonapoulos, un personaje sordo, es enviado a un manicomio estatal, dejando atrás a su único amigo, John Singer.</p>

<p>La escena transmite una sensación palpable de angustia y tristeza. Además, despierta una ira justificada hacia el primo de Antonapoulos por haberlo alejado, una decisión motivada por la conveniencia y basada en un malentendido que interpreta las dificultades de Spiros como un comportamiento desviado y antisocial. El hecho de que provenga de una familia de inmigrantes y viva en un pequeño pueblo de Georgia le da a la escena un matiz aún más intenso.</p>

<p>ChatGPT, sin embargo, describió la escena utilizando una terminología estéril y abstracta. Para citar una respuesta representativa que compartió uno de mis alumnos: «La atmósfera es devastadoramente solitaria y parece suspendida en el tiempo. La escena se percibe como tranquila, desamparada y emocionalmente unilateral. No hay una despedida dramática; en cambio, el momento está marcado por la angustia silenciosa de Singer. La partida del tren simboliza una separación irreversible».</p>

<p>La descripción es fría y objetiva. No logra captar el peso de la profunda tristeza que emana de la separación de dos amigos que solo se tienen el uno al otro. Además, contiene un error factual: es un autobús, no un tren, el que se aleja.</p>

<p>También falta un reconocimiento claro del temor de Singer ante los horrores que le esperan a Antonapoulos, así como de la ironía dramática que genera la aparente inconsciencia de Antonapoulos respecto a cómo su vida está siendo trastornada. La IA simplemente carece de la experiencia vivida necesaria para desarrollar <a href="https://sbmi.uth.edu/blog/2024/artificial-intelligence-versus-human-intelligence.htm">conciencia contextual</a> de manera que le permita comprender verdaderamente la inquietante novela de McCullers.</p>

<p>Dado que la IA funciona en gran medida como un <a href="https://www.forbes.com/sites/joetoscano1/2025/09/03/ai-is-destroying-seo-rank-now-requires-answer-engine-optimization/">motor de optimización</a> —basándose en la síntesis de enormes cantidades de datos en línea y en el resumen de los resultados—, sus análisis de esta escena y de otras fueron sistemáticamente superficiales; «carecían de profundidad» y estaban llenos de «tópicos vagos», como lo expresaron dos estudiantes. </p>

<h2>Acceder a la experiencia corporal</h2>

<p>A continuación, les pedí a mis alumnos que le pidieran a la IA que generara “una nueva escena con al menos tres personajes” de su elección.</p>

<p>El resultado creativo fue aún más insípido. A los alumnos les divirtió especialmente que la IA hiciera que John Singer, quien actúa como un eje que conecta a todos los demás personajes, hablara sobre una variedad de temas. El problema, por supuesto, es que Singer, al igual que Antonapoulos, también es sordo. </p>

<figure class="align-center ">
            <img alt="Fotograma de una película en el que aparece un hombre sentado, vestido con traje, con los ojos cerrados, la cabeza inclinada hacia abajo y las manos levantadas." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/754372/original/file-20260817-69-uclkfj.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/754372/original/file-20260817-69-uclkfj.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=334&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/754372/original/file-20260817-69-uclkfj.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=334&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/754372/original/file-20260817-69-uclkfj.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=334&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/754372/original/file-20260817-69-uclkfj.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=420&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/754372/original/file-20260817-69-uclkfj.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=420&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/754372/original/file-20260817-69-uclkfj.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=420&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px">
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Alan Arkin interpreta a John Singer en la adaptación cinematográfica de 1968 de «El corazón es un cazador solitario».</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://nitrateglow.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/02/image-5.png">Warner Bros.</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>No es de extrañar que esa IA no pudiera comprender la experiencia de no poder oír. Es importante recordar que interactuar con una IA significa tratar con una <a href="https://www.sainsburywellcome.org/blog/ai-embodiment-and-neuroscience">inteligencia sintética</a> que carece de un cuerpo a través del cual experimentar e interactuar con el mundo.</p>

<p>Sin una presencia física, no puede ponerse en el lugar de sus usuarios ni experimentar nada que se acerque a la empatía humana. Si bien los multimillonarios de la tecnología, como Elon Musk y Marc Andreessen, pueden <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2025/05/04/opinion/empathy-ethics.html">considerar la empatía y la introspección como debilidades</a>, esos rasgos son el corazón palpitante de la literatura y el arte, la fuente de la creatividad y la conexión humana.</p>

<p>En otras palabras, la emoción, la empatía y la irracionalidad podrían considerarse algunos de los contrapisos más poderosos frente a la IA.</p>



<h2>Aceptar la fragilidad humana</h2>

<p>Puede haber situaciones en las que la IA resulte útil para mis alumnos, <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=h4NAygTNago">y creo que los esfuerzos por prohibir el uso de la IA</a> son inviables y contraproducentes. </p>

<p>La posibilidad de prescindir por completo de estas herramientas es, en gran medida, un lujo. Así como muchas personas no pueden permitirse contratar a alguien para que limpie su casa, cuide su jardín o cuide a sus hijos, quienes luchan por llegar a fin de mes <a href="https://www.cgdev.org/blog/how-do-poorest-use-ai">quizá necesiten recurrir a la ayuda de la IA</a>.</p>

<p>Pero mi esperanza es que mis alumnos —especialmente en lo que respecta a su trabajo intelectual— comprendan que el uso de la tecnología implica renunciar a capacidades que son esenciales para el pensamiento y la creatividad humanos: la imaginación, la intuición y la autorreflexión.</p>

<p>Quiero que lo piensen dos veces antes de intentar ocultar, con un chatbot, las fragilidades, debilidades, obsesiones y divagaciones inherentes a la mente humana. En cambio, quiero que acepten estas tendencias humanas y se entreguen a lo que el poeta William Wordsworth llamó el «<a href="https://www.poetryfoundation.org/articles/91748/william-wordsworth-101">desbordamiento espontáneo de sentimientos poderosos</a>». </p>

<p>Después de todo, el mejor arte suele surgir de quienes se encuentran en su momento de mayor vulnerabilidad, confusión y desorientación.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/292126/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

Los investigadores ya están documentando estos efectos , que amenazan con convertir el esfuerzo de lidiar con las ideas en un arte perdido
Por eso creo que es fundamental que los educadores enfrenten la IA de frente

La clave, en mi opinión, es enseñar a los estudiantes a distinguir las habilidades de reconocimiento de patrones de la IA de su incapacidad para soñar despierta, ponerse en el lugar de los demás y expresarse de manera auténtica
Dime qué piensas En un curso que impartí recientemente sobre literatura gótica sureña, les propuse un ejercicio a mis alumnos
Se les pidió que le pidieran a la IA que analizara la «atmósfera emocional» de una escena de la novela de Carson McCullers de 1940, « El corazón es un cazador solitario »
Muchos de los personajes que los lectores conocen en las obras del gótico sureño , como las de McCullers, son extravagantes y brutales

Retratados desde una perspectiva distorsionada y antinatural, hablan en dialectos extraños y evocan lo que Flannery O’Connor se refirió al « grotesco .» Viven en lugares aislados que parecen anclados en el pasado y que, por usar otra expresión de O’Connor, están « perseguidos por Cristo »
A muchos lectores les cuesta asimilar los extraños mundos de estos personajes
A la IA le resulta aún más difícil generalizar las complejas tensiones entre la fe y la incredulidad, o entre el bien y el mal, que dan vida a estas historias
AP Photo Para limitar el abanico de respuestas y permitir comparaciones útiles, les proporcioné a los estudiantes escenas en las que aparecían los personajes principales de la novela
Una de ellas era la secuencia desgarradora en la que Spiros Antonapoulos, un personaje sordo, es enviado a un manicomio estatal, dejando atrás a su único amigo, John Singer
La escena transmite una sensación palpable de angustia y tristeza

Además, despierta una ira justificada hacia el primo de Antonapoulos por haberlo alejado, una decisión motivada por la conveniencia y basada en un malentendido que interpreta las dificultades de Spiros como un comportamiento desviado y antisocial
El hecho de que provenga de una familia de inmigrantes y viva en un pequeño pueblo de Georgia le da a la escena un matiz aún más intenso
ChatGPT, sin embargo, describió la escena utilizando una terminología estéril y abstracta
Para citar una respuesta representativa que compartió uno de mis alumnos: «La atmósfera es devastadoramente solitaria y parece suspendida en el tiempo
La escena se percibe como tranquila, desamparada y emocionalmente unilateral
No hay una despedida dramática; en cambio, el momento está marcado por la angustia silenciosa de Singer
La partida del tren simboliza una separación irreversible»
No logra captar el peso de la profunda tristeza que emana de la separación de dos amigos que solo se tienen el uno al otro
Además, contiene un error factual: es un autobús, no un tren, el que se aleja

También falta un reconocimiento claro del temor de Singer ante los horrores que le esperan a Antonapoulos, así como de la ironía dramática que genera la aparente inconsciencia de Antonapoulos respecto a cómo su vida está siendo trastornada
La IA simplemente carece de la experiencia vivida necesaria para desarrollar conciencia contextual de manera que le permita comprender verdaderamente la inquietante novela de McCullers

Dado que la IA funciona en gran medida como un motor de optimización —basándose en la síntesis de enormes cantidades de datos en línea y en el resumen de los resultados—, sus análisis de esta escena y de otras fueron sistemáticamente superficiales; «carecían de profundidad» y estaban llenos de «tópicos vagos», como lo expresaron dos estudiantes
Acceder a la experiencia corporal A continuación, les pedí a mis alumnos que le pidieran a la IA que generara “una nueva escena con al menos tres personajes” de su elección
El resultado creativo fue aún más insípido
A los alumnos les divirtió especialmente que la IA hiciera que John Singer, quien actúa como un eje que conecta a todos los demás personajes, hablara sobre una variedad de temas
El problema, por supuesto, es que Singer, al igual que Antonapoulos, también es sordo
Alan Arkin interpreta a John Singer en la adaptación cinematográfica de 1968 de «El corazón es un cazador solitario»
No es de extrañar que esa IA no pudiera comprender la experiencia de no poder oír
Es importante recordar que interactuar con una IA significa tratar con una inteligencia sintética que carece de un cuerpo a través del cual experimentar e interactuar con el mundo
Sin una presencia física, no puede ponerse en el lugar de sus usuarios ni experimentar nada que se acerque a la empatía humana

Si bien los multimillonarios de la tecnología, como Elon Musk y Marc Andreessen, pueden considerar la empatía y la introspección como debilidades , esos rasgos son el corazón palpitante de la literatura y el arte, la fuente de la creatividad y la conexión humana

<title>Iran war pushes diesel – the economy’s lifeblood – to record high prices, with no relief on the horizon</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760249/original/file-20260916-50-6bf50u.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C5000%2C3333&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Diesel fuel prices are at all-time highs in the United States.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/sign-displays-the-prices-of-regular-gasoline-and-diesel-at-news-photo/2294723764">Paul Weaver/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Diesel fuel prices in the U.S. continue to break all-time records, <a href="https://www.eia.gov/petroleum/gasdiesel/">hitting $6.28 a gallon</a> as a national average on Sept. 14, 2026, and they aren’t likely to come down anytime soon. Because diesel is the fuel for freight transportation, farming and construction – and is related to a key heating fuel – the effects are set to spread across the entire U.S. economy.</p>

<p>The inflation-adjusted price of diesel in late August was <a href="https://usenergydata.org/charts/gasoline-prices/?tab=chart&amp;fuel=diesel&amp;time=2011..2026&amp;areas=NUS%7ESCA">about as high as it was in 2022</a> and has likely risen further. There are still three factors that we, scholars of U.S. and <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=DAwwVkwAAAAJ&amp;hl=en&amp;oi=ao">global energy markets</a> and <a href="https://payneinstitute.mines.edu/project/jamie-webster/">supply chains</a>, see that set the stage for prices to remain high and potentially climb even further. </p>

<p>Two of these elements – environmental protection regulations on oil refineries and <a href="https://www.cnbc.com/2026/09/14/trump-ukraine-russia-diesel-prices-oil.html">Russia’s war with Ukraine</a> – have been building tension for years. But the situation has been pushed into a crisis by the <a href="https://www.wsj.com/business/energy-oil/americans-have-spent-100-billion-more-on-fuel-during-the-iran-war-377952a1">U.S. war against Iran</a>, which has closed the Strait of Hormuz to a large percentage of oil and refined products shipments for more than six months.</p>

<p>Amid that crisis, U.S. oil refineries are <a href="https://financialpost.com/pmn/business-pmn/us-refiners-see-billions-in-profits-from-global-fuel-crunch">making lots of money</a>.</p>

<p>In mid-September 2026, diesel prices were up 67% over <a href="https://www.bts.gov/newsroom/motor-fuel-prices-september-2025-0">September 2025’s monthly national average of $3.75 a gallon</a>, and they have risen sharply since. In January 2026, before the U.S. and Israel first attacked Iran in late February, the average diesel price in the U.S. was lower, <a href="https://www.bts.gov/newsroom/motor-fuel-prices-january-2026-1">at $3.52 a gallon</a> – meaning that diesel prices have jumped more than 78% since the war began.</p>

<p>In part, that’s because the country, and the world, have been losing diesel refining capacity for many years and can’t just ramp up production to fill the shortages.</p>

            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760252/original/file-20260916-70-tk3jz9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A person standing next to a large truck pumps fuel into a tank." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760252/original/file-20260916-70-tk3jz9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760252/original/file-20260916-70-tk3jz9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=399&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760252/original/file-20260916-70-tk3jz9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=399&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760252/original/file-20260916-70-tk3jz9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=399&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760252/original/file-20260916-70-tk3jz9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=502&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760252/original/file-20260916-70-tk3jz9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=502&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760252/original/file-20260916-70-tk3jz9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=502&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Diesel prices hit truckers, who deliver a vast range of products to consumers and markets across the nation.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/person-pumps-diesel-at-a-pilot-gas-station-on-september-14-news-photo/2295291579">Brandon Bell/Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Refinery capacity drops</h2>

<p>Starting in 2006, U.S. federal regulations were phased in that required refiners to produce diesel fuel with far less sulfur than had previously been allowed. The regulations were intended to reduce <a href="https://www.epa.gov/archive/epapages/newsroom_archive/newsreleases/f8c41d888050eb7c85257188006f8f47.html">air pollution and acid rain precursors mainly from trucks and buses</a>. The <a href="https://www.farmprogress.com/management/diesel-fuel-s-successful-transition-to-ultra-low-sulfur">resulting fuel was much cleaner</a>. In 2014, the rules were applied to locomotives and marine vehicles. </p>

<p>U.S. refineries had to install expensive equipment to comply, which took <a href="https://www.ogj.com/refining-processing/article/17224535/questions-linger-as-refiners-cut-us-diesel-sulfur-content">years and billions of dollars</a>. This, in turn, increased costs <a href="https://www.ezoil.com/resources-diesel-ultra-low-sulfur-diesel-basics">between 5 and 9 cents per gallon</a>. And the fuel <a href="https://www.ezoil.com/resources-diesel-ultra-low-sulfur-diesel-basics">contains slightly less energy</a> per unit of volume – so a larger quantity of low-sulfur diesel is required to meet the demand.</p>

<p>Only one refinery, <a href="https://inspectioneering.com/news/2019-08-28/8725/texas-storage-terminal-operator-plans-to-build-its-own-refinery">in Galveston, Texas</a>, has been built <a href="https://www.opis.com/resources/energy-market-news-from-opis/us-total-refining-capacity-down-again-in-2025-after-two-refinery-shutdowns-eia/">in the past 50 years</a>, and at 45,000 barrels per day it meets less than 0.2% of U.S. demand. In 2025, two <a href="https://www.eia.gov/todayinenergy/detail.php?id=67807">refineries shut down</a> due to poor economic performance. And since 2020, more than a dozen others have <a href="https://www.mckinsey.com/industries/oil-and-gas/our-insights/converting-refineries-to-renewable-fuels-no-simple-switch">converted to producing renewable diesel</a> to take advantage of federal and state biofuel incentives, but that conversion can cut the amount of actual fuel they produce at least in half, according to our estimates.</p>

<p>As a result, the remaining refineries are running flat out. Crude going into refineries reached <a href="https://www.agbull.com/diesel-gets-a-small-reprieve-but-refinery-slack-is-nearly-gone/">about 17.5 million barrels a day</a> in late August, and refineries were operating at nearly 98% of their maximum capacity – the highest level since 2018. Even so, <a href="https://www.eia.gov/tools/glossary/index.php?id=Distillate%20fuel%20oil">output of distillate</a>, which includes diesel and related fuels such as heating oil and jet fuel, was lower than in 2025.</p>

<p>Distillate inventories held by refiners, distributors and retailers <a href="https://rbnenergy.com/daily-posts/blog/100bbl-diesel-crack-or-how-2026-exposed-fragility-global-refining">fell to about 103 million barrels</a> by late August, the lowest for that point in the calendar since 1951.</p>

<p><iframe id="OMEBT" class="tc-infographic-datawrapper" src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/OMEBT/1/" height="400px" width="100%" style="border: 0;" scrolling="no" frameborder="0" title="A line chart showing the percentage of capacity in operation of U.S. oil refineries."></iframe></p>

<h2>A global squeeze</h2>

<p>As U.S. inventories of diesel fell in August, the <a href="https://oilprice.com/Latest-Energy-News/World-News/US-Diesel-Exports-Hit-Record-High-as-Domestic-Stockpiles-Slide.html">country’s diesel exports hit a record high</a> as the global market sought to fill supplies normally provided by Russia.</p>

<p>Historically the world’s <a href="https://universaltrades.co/blog/top-10-diesel-exporting-countries-en/">second-largest diesel exporter</a> after the United States, Russia <a href="https://www.spglobal.com/energy/en/news-research/latest-news/crude-oil/072726-russia-extends-gasoline-export-ban-until-end-of-2026/">banned exports of diesel on July 9, 2026</a>, to ensure supplies for its military. In September, the country extended the export ban until the end of 2026 in the wake of <a href="https://www.washingtonpost.com/business/2026/09/04/diesel-hits-record-585-gallon-iran-war-drags/">Ukrainian drone strikes</a> on Russian refineries. </p>

<p>Middle Eastern refiners, also key to global diesel supplies, have scaled back production because of <a href="https://www.reuters.com/commentary/reuters-open-interest/trumps-ukraine-energy-truce-wont-fix-global-diesel-crunch-2026-09-15/">disruptions from the war with Iran</a>.</p>

<p>Together, these forces mean the <a href="https://www.eia.gov/petroleum/gasdiesel/">supply for diesel is very tight</a>.</p>

<p>On Sept. 15, 2026, U.S. Senate Majority Leader <a href="https://www.morningstar.com/news/marketwatch/20260915132/top-senate-republican-floats-a-diesel-export-ban-as-prices-soar-it-might-not-work">John Thune proposed the U.S. ban diesel exports</a> to increase domestic availability.</p>

<h2>Refiners seek dollars</h2>

<p>Even before the crisis in the Persian Gulf, the U.S. Energy Information Administration reported several factors were pushing diesel prices upward, including <a href="https://www.eia.gov/todayinenergy/detail.php?id=67184">large exports to Europe</a>, a <a href="https://www.eia.gov/petroleum/heatingoilpropane/#itn-tabs-2">cold winter in the Northeast</a> in 2025-26 and <a href="https://www.eia.gov/outlooks/aeo/narrative/">high freight demand</a>.</p>

<p>With the war continuing, refinery companies are taking advantage of the low supply – and their <a href="https://rbnenergy.com/daily-posts/blog/us-refiners-already-running-hard-relief-diesel-remains-elusive">inability to make a whole lot more diesel</a> – to charge <a href="https://www.eia.gov/todayinenergy/detail.php?id=68104">more than ever</a> for diesel fuel.</p>

<p>By late August, short-term profit margins for making diesel – called “<a href="https://www.eia.gov/todayinenergy/includes/crackspread_explain.php">crack spreads</a>” in the industry – <a href="https://finance.yahoo.com/energy/articles/100-diesel-cracks-signal-much-200000054.html">surpassed $100 per barrel</a> for the first time ever, clearly showing demand for the fuel is well outpacing supply, as well as demand for crude oil itself.</p>

<p>What this means is that truckers, drivers and shipping companies are paying more for diesel – costs that are passed on to consumers. At the same time, <a href="https://financialpost.com/pmn/business-pmn/us-refiners-see-billions-in-profits-from-global-fuel-crunch">refinery companies are seeing large profits</a>.</p>

<p><iframe id="G9ocE" class="tc-infographic-datawrapper" src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/G9ocE/2/" height="400px" width="100%" style="border: 0;" scrolling="no" frameborder="0" title="A map of the US showing per-capita spending on diesel and related fuels by state in 2024."></iframe></p>

<h2>High diesel prices hit everyone</h2>

<p>The vast majority of the diesel fuel used in the U.S. is for transportation, <a href="https://www.atlanticcouncil.org/blogs/energysource/the-diesel-shock-is-here-which-us-states-will-be-hit-the-hardest">mostly trucking</a>. Other significant users are the railroad, agriculture, construction and marine industries. </p>

<p>A <a href="https://www.kttc.com/2026/09/07/diesel-prices-drive-up-harvest-costs-minnesota-iowa-farmers/">congressional Joint Economic Committee analysis</a> in September 2026 found that higher diesel prices added more than $1.4 billion to the cost of planting major U.S. crops in 2026 versus 2025, a 63% increase, with Illinois, Iowa and Minnesota hit hardest. Because nearly every retail item travels by truck at some point, the diesel spike also feeds slowly into broader consumer inflation.</p>

<p>And there’s one more hit coming: Heating oil, which is chemically closely related to diesel, is a <a href="https://www.eia.gov/outlooks/steo/report/perspectives/2025/10-winterfuels/2025_winter_fuels.pdf">key heating fuel</a> in the northeastern U.S. The latest projection from the Energy Information Administration expects national distillate inventories to <a href="https://www.eia.gov/outlooks/steo/">fall below 100 million barrels</a> in September and stay at that level through much of 2027. That’s lower than it has been since 2021, and heating oil prices for the coming winter are <a href="https://abc17news.com/money/cnn-business-consumer/2026/09/14/get-ready-for-a-30-jump-in-heating-oil-costs-this-winter-as-iran-war-drives-up-prices/">already up 30% or more</a>.</p>

<p>The Middle East conflict is having wide-reaching implications. While crude oil prices are now above $100 per barrel, it is diesel, the fuel that much of the economy runs on, that is feeling the greatest stress.</p>

<p>And as refiners run flat out, any interruption would reduce production, as happened after a power outage at a <a href="https://www.reuters.com/business/energy/exxon-mobils-joliet-refinery-reports-upset-due-power-outage-2026-09-14/">Mobil refinery in Illinois</a> on Sept. 13.</p>

<p>With falling stockpiles, even a sudden end to the Iran war is unlikely to yield significantly lower prices anytime soon.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/292049/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760309/original/file-20260916-50-buyyaa.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=225%2C329%2C3867%2C2578&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Yemen&#39;s Houthi armed forces patrol the capital Sanaa on Sept. 12, 2026.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/yemens-houthi-armed-forces-patrol-as-yemeni-prisoners-loyal-news-photo/2294384190?adppopup=true">Mohammed Huwaish/AFP via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>It took just a few days for Houthi forces to <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/sep/15/houthi-rebels-seize-red-sea-hanish-islands-saudi-oil-warning">seize most of Yemen’s Red Sea coast</a>, including the <a href="https://www.aljazeera.com/economy/2026/9/13/red-sea-nations-watch-as-houthis-seize-bab-al-mandeb-strait">shores of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait</a>, a crucial Red Sea maritime choke point. </p>

<p>The offensive started on Sept. 3, 2026, with a push to cut the strategically important road linking the city of Taiz to the port of Mokha. By Sept. 11, Mokha, the town of Dhubab and the island of Mayyun, in the mouth of the strait, <a href="https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/c4g7vr0lngwo">were under Houthi control</a>.</p>

<p>The Yemeni rebel group seized <a href="https://abcnews.com/International/houthis-yemen-gains-put-control-strategic-strait-key/story?id=136485092">some 2,100 square miles of territory</a>, forcing <a href="https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/9/15/more-than-100000-displaced-as-they-flee-violence-in-yemen-un">more than 100,000 people</a> to flee, according to the U.N., with many making the risky journey to nearby Djibouti by boats. </p>

<p>It is the largest shift in the front lines of Yemen’s civil war since a <a href="https://news.un.org/en/story/2022/04/1116282">U.N.-brokered truce</a> froze them in April 2022.</p>

<p>Most of the coverage has interpreted the offensive <a href="https://www.economist.com/middle-east-and-africa/2026/09/13/the-houthis-shock-advance-in-yemen-gives-iran-new-leverage">as a new lever for Iran</a> – a key ally of the Houthis – in its ongoing war with the United States, or a <a href="https://www.reuters.com/world/middle-east/houthis-strike-saudi-targets-anew-talks-over-strait-hormuz-stall-2026-09-15/">fresh threat to Saudi Arabia</a> and global shipping. </p>

<p>Such framing is not wrong, but it is incomplete. The more consequential question, I believe, is what the offensive means for Yemen itself, and where it leaves both a civil war that had quietly stalemated for years and the Houthis’ own unresolved problem of legitimacy.</p>

<h2>Why advance now?</h2>

<p>Years of Yemeni civil strife entered a new phase in 2014 when <a href="https://www.bbc.com/news/world-29380668">Houthis seized the capital Sanaa</a> from the increasingly unpopular government of President Abdrabbuh Mansur Hadi. </p>

<p>A decade of subsequent fighting between the rebel group and a Saudi-led coalition <a href="https://wfpusa.org/place/yemen/">brought famine</a> and destruction across the impoverished nation. But since 2022 the conflict has largely been stalled, with Houthis controlling much of the country’s northwest and the Saudi-backed forces remaining dominant in parts of the country’s south and east. </p>

<p><iframe id="7bAJT" class="tc-infographic-datawrapper" src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/7bAJT/2/" height="400px" width="100%" style="border: 0;" scrolling="no" frameborder="0" title="A map of the Persian Gulf region"></iframe></p>

<p>So why have the Houthis advanced now? The group’s military spokesman, Yahya Saree, <a href="https://www.pbs.org/newshour/show/iran-backed-houthis-seize-island-at-entrance-to-red-sea-threatening-saudi-oil-export">said it was triggered</a> by years of Saudi aggression and blockade.</p>

<p>Such grievances are not invented. U.N. agencies have documented real, sustained damage from <a href="https://news.un.org/en/story/2017/11/570122">coalition restrictions on Yemen’s ports and airspace</a> over the course of the civil war.</p>

<p>The Houthis also trace the latest round of fighting to a <a href="https://www.nbcnews.com/world/yemen/yemen-saudi-arabia-air-strike-sanna-airport-houthi-rebels-rcna587273">July 13 strike on the Sanaa airport’s runway</a> by Yemeni government forces with Saudi backing. That attack forced an Iranian aircraft carrying officers of Iran’s powerful <a href="https://www.cfr.org/backgrounders/irans-revolutionary-guards">Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps</a> to turn back.</p>

<p>The Houthis declared their ceasefire with Saudi Arabia over that day, <a href="https://apnews.com/article/yemen-houthis-airport-saudi-strikes-7bddae3006304df8bf7f89e980006b33">struck the airport of the Saudi city of Abha</a> within hours and announced a naval blockade a week later. They then opened a missile campaign in early August, well before the ground offensive on Sept. 3. </p>

<p>But it is hard to read the Houthis’ sustained campaign and the landings on Bab el-Mandeb’s islands as simple payback for an airport strike. Rather, something more deliberate appears to have been in motion.</p>

<p>Another factor is Iran. Since Tehran <a href="https://www.brookings.edu/articles/why-irans-disruption-of-the-strait-of-hormuz-matters/">closed the Strait of Hormuz</a> in March following the U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran, Saudi Arabia has routed crude oil through Bab el-Mandeb at roughly eight times the rate it did a year earlier. </p>

<p>Houthi control of that strait hands Iran a mirror-image choke point to the one it has over Hormuz. Indeed, Yemeni security sources say a <a href="https://www.thenationalnews.com/news/mena/2026/09/14/shadow-man-irgc-flight-and-a-secret-meeting-irans-hand-in-houthi-offensive-revealed/">senior Iranian commander, Abdul Reza Shahlai</a>, was on the ground overseeing part of the latest operation in September.</p>

<p>There’s also a potential economic incentive for the Houthis. Since March, Tehran has been <a href="https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-03-24/iran-charges-some-ships-hormuz-transit-fees-for-safe-passage">charging vessels up to US$2 million a ship</a> for safe passage through Hormuz. The Houthis may likewise see economic leverage as a way to bolster a movement long battered by war.</p>

<h2>Forcing Riyadh back to that table</h2>

<p>Perhaps the most important factor, however, is that the Houthis reasoned conditions on the ground were increasingly favorable for an offensive. Their already fractured opposition has become even more divided in the country’s south, particularly after a <a href="https://www.foreignaffairs.com/united-states/real-risks-saudi-uae-feud">Saudi rift with the United Arab Emirates in late 2025</a> led the latter to withdraw its support for anti-Houthi forces in the south altogether. </p>

<p>With the broader region engulfed in conflict and Saudi Arabia distracted, the Houthis made their move against a coastal Yemeni force that has been left exposed.</p>

<p>First and foremost, the Houthis are a Yemeni movement whose fight has always been about power inside Yemen. As such, Houthi officials have been careful to frame the Bab el-Mandeb operation as a national, sovereign act rather than one done for its Iranian ally; they are adamant that they are <a href="https://nationalinterest.org/blog/middle-east-watch/why-the-houthis-are-not-an-iranian-proxy">not a mere Iranian proxy</a>.</p>

<p>As recently as 2023, Saudi Arabia and the Houthis had been negotiating a <a href="https://www.cfr.org/global-conflict-tracker/conflict/war-yemen">comprehensive nationwide ceasefire</a> that would have, in part, ended Saudi restrictions and sanctions on Houthi governance. But the plan was never implemented following the <a href="https://documents1.worldbank.org/curated/en/099253002102539789/pdf/IDU10b8b59671dbc814cfc19c4a1299ff54854ba.pdf">Red Sea crisis of late 2023 and 2024</a>, when the Houthis ramped up attacks on commercial shipping in response to the Israeli war in Gaza. Riyadh has shown little urgency to revive the diplomatic process since.</p>

<p>The Houthis may now be betting that escalating inside Yemen, where the cost to Saudi Arabia is high, is the surest way to force Riyadh back to that table. This time, they may believe they have leverage to receive the political recognition they have wanted all along, not just the <a href="https://south24.net/news/news.php?nid=5481">economic terms Saudi Arabia was considering</a> in 2023.</p>

<figure class="align-center ">
            <img alt="A black plume of sm okes rises from the desert." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760315/original/file-20260916-50-nz778c.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760315/original/file-20260916-50-nz778c.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=373&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760315/original/file-20260916-50-nz778c.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=373&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760315/original/file-20260916-50-nz778c.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=373&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760315/original/file-20260916-50-nz778c.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=469&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760315/original/file-20260916-50-nz778c.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=469&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/760315/original/file-20260916-50-nz778c.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=469&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px">

            </figcaption>
