<h2>What the Strait operation cannot buy</h2>

<p>The seizure of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait and the ongoing fighting in the country come with serious risks for the Houthis, however. The leverage the Houthis are gaining vis-a-vis Saudi Arabia and on the battlefield in Yemen could come at the cost of their broader standing in Yemen. </p>

<p>No government or entity has ever managed to hold both military and political supremacy over the entire territory of Yemen <a href="https://www.britannica.com/place/Yemen/Government-and-society">in modern history</a>. While the Houthis have achieved military supremacy in the vast majority of the northwest, they have never pursued anything resembling a political bargain with the internationally backed government or even other parties. Their movement has always prized military dominance over political inclusion. </p>

<p>The latest coastal offensive is no exception. </p>

<p>According to Houthi-affiliated news sources, within days of taking Mokha the group <a href="https://www.yemenipress.net/archives/439895">had moved to reopen the port’s customs house</a>, <a href="https://masa-press.net/2026/09/10/%D8%A3%D9%88%D9%84%D9%89-%D8%A7%D9%84%D8%A8%D8%B4%D8%A7%D8%A6%D8%B1-%D8%B9%D9%84%D9%89-%D9%85%D9%8A%D9%86%D8%A7%D8%A1-%D8%A7%D9%84%D9%85%D8%AE%D8%A7-%D8%AA%D8%AE%D9%81%D9%8A%D8%B6%D8%A7%D8%AA-%D8%AA/">cut port fees and customs duties by as much as half</a> and <a href="https://www.yemenipress.net/archives/439918">launched a drive to hand out 20,000 food baskets across Mokha and the neighboring coastal districts</a>, while its authority in Sanaa <a href="https://www.ypagency.net/890001">offered a general amnesty</a> to the fighters who had held the coast against it. A week later, its leader, Abdulmalik al-Houthi, <a href="https://www.ypagency.net/891898">told southerners directly</a> that his forces were not targeting them, only the troops Saudi Arabia had brought in. </p>

<p>That is legitimacy performed through governance after a military conquest, more public relations than policy. It certainly isn’t the political bargain that could hold Yemen together for long. Moreover, a decade of Houthi rule in Sanaa suggests that they have no desire to work with others. Their modus operandi has been to rule by guns, not coalition. </p>

<p>More broadly, seizing the Arabian Peninsula’s other choke point and banning Saudi shipping through it makes the Houthis look, to much of the world and no small part of Yemen, like Tehran’s instrument – whatever their own objectives actually are.</p>

<p>And it invites the Houthis’ enemies to respond with force, potentially weakening the group’s capabilities.</p>

<p>Saudi Arabia is not a neutral party waiting patiently for good sense to prevail. It has prosecuted the war in Yemen for over a decade at <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2018/10/26/world/middleeast/saudi-arabia-war-yemen.html">enormous cost to the country’s civilians</a>. Few in Yemen expect the Saudi-backed government to try retaking Sanaa by force, and a negotiated settlement will most likely be necessary eventually. But the Houthis have certainly now exposed themselves – and any Yemeni civilians caught up in escalation – to relentless <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/15/world/middleeast/yemen-saudi-arabia-houthis-attacks.html">airstrikes by Saudi Arabia</a> and its allies.</p>

<p>For the Houthis, the gamble to advance now may backfire. It is one thing to take territory and quite another thing to hold it. Moreover, the Houthis may now find themselves controlling a strait the world wants reopened while still lacking the one thing that strait was never going to buy them: a whole country that actually consents to their rule.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/291930/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<title>The story of Little Italy’s Feast of San Gennaro is the story of how Italian immigrants became American</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760297/original/file-20260916-50-cd1knd.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C6000%2C3999&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Over the past century, New York City&#39;s Feast of San Gennaro has grown from a one-day, parochial affair into an 11-day event that draws more than a million visitors.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/participants-march-in-the-grand-procession-parade-at-the-news-photo/2235253553?adppopup=true">Spencer Platt/Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>For two weeks in September, everyone wants to be Italian – at least judging by the crowds at the annual <a href="https://sangennaronyc.org/">Feast of San Gennaro</a> in New York City’s Little Italy. </p>

<p>Founded in 1926, the largest and longest-running Italian festival in the United States celebrates its 100th anniversary this year, with locals and tourists alike descending upon Mulberry Street in Manhattan to celebrate Italian American culture.</p>

<p>To be sure, there’s plenty that’s commercialized: Frank Sinatra impersonators croon “New York, New York,” while vendors hawk shirts with quotes from “The Godfather” and “The Sopranos” at astronomical prices. Classic Italian American fare like chicken parm subs and sausage and peppers fly off food carts.</p>

<p>And yet in my work <a href="https://www.history.ox.ac.uk/people/clare-whitton">as a medievalist</a>, I’ve explored how this festival champions traditions that go back thousands of years.</p>

<p>If anything, the fact that centuries-old rituals coexist with sweet Italian sausages and big, floppy pizza slices speaks to a lengthy, strenuous and beautiful process of cultural assimilation.</p>

<h2>From the Bay of Naples to Little Italy</h2>

<p>Between 1881 and 1920, over <a href="https://www.routledge.com/The-Routledge-History-of-Italian-Americans/Connell-Pugliese/p/book/9780367230937">4.5 million Italians</a> immigrated to America. Thousands, most of whom hailed from southern Italy, settled on Manhattan’s Lower East Side to form what became <a href="https://www.digitalgreensboro.org/record/15655?p=%28+%28subject%3A%28cultural+%2B+identity%29%29%29&amp;v=pdf">Little Italy</a>. </p>

<p>These “<a href="https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poems/46550/the-new-colossus">huddled masses</a>” faced all sorts of difficulties: overcrowded tenements, trouble finding work, racial discrimination and <a href="https://doi.org/10.1057/9780230115323_4">suspicion of their southern Italian Catholic practices</a>, particularly from Irish Catholics. The Italian procession of religious statues and the street parties that followed, the Irish argued, looked far too pagan and idolatrous to be considered “real” Catholicism. Irish suspicion of such practices were also shared by local Protestants.</p>

<p>But by the early 20th century, Italian communities had grown so large that they could <a href="https://services.publishing.umich.edu/Books/T/The-Ruin-of-Souls2">fund their own Italian-speaking churches</a>.</p>

<p>One such parish was the <a href="https://oldcathedral.org/shrine-church-of-the-most-precious-blood">Church of the Most Precious Blood</a>, built in 1904 on Baxter Street. In 1926, a group of parishioners led by <a href="https://www.nydailynews.com/2010/07/17/how-street-it-is-for-kings-of-the-fair-as-producers-get-lions-share-from-cookie-cutter-fests/">Alexander Tisi</a> organized a tribute to one of the most popular holy figures from southern Italy: St. Januarius, known in Italian as San Gennaro.</p>

<p>An early Christian bishop, Gennaro <a href="https://gallica.bnf.fr/ark:/12148/bpt6k314988h/f3.item">was brutally beheaded</a> outside of Naples on Sept. 19 in AD 305 on account of his faith. His execution was one of several that took place during the <a href="https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/religion-and-philosophy/diocletianic-persecution">Diocletian Persecutions</a>, a systematic campaign against Christians by the Roman Empire.</p>

<p>Since then, southern Italians have attributed <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2009/09/21/world/europe/21iht-naples.html">all sorts of miracles</a> to his intercession, including extinguishing <a href="https://repositori.udl.cat/server/api/core/bitstreams/3a649f23-e6d4-473a-8147-2e7f84cb3860/content">the volcanic fires of Mount Vesuvius</a> in 1631.</p>

<p>He is also seen as something of a prophet. <a href="https://www.routledge.com/The-Natural-History-of-a-Neapolitan-Miracle-The-Secret-of-San-Gennaros-Blood/deCeglia/p/book/9781032442617">Since at least 1389</a>, two vials purportedly containing the <a href="https://theconversation.com/what-makes-religious-relics-like-pieces-of-the-true-cross-and-hair-of-saints-sacred-to-christians-181699">saint’s blood</a> have been venerated in Naples because of their inexplicable <a href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/1479851">ability to liquefy</a> on his feast days. <a href="https://italoamericano.org/curiosities-san-gennaro/">The liquefaction has long been interpreted</a> as a sign of the saint’s protection. On the other hand, Italians viewed the blood staying solid as the sign of a looming catastrophe. The <a href="https://historiamag.com/the-liberation-of-naples-in-1943-and-its-dire-consequences/">Allied bombings of Naples in 1943</a>, for example, occurred after the blood failed to liquefy.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">

<p>Since the later Middle Ages, Gennaro’s feast on Sept. 19 has been <a href="https://doi.org/10.1017/9781108779555.004">one of the most important dates</a> on Naples’ calendar.</p>

<p>During medieval and Renaissance celebrations, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1017/9781805432456">pork was the meal of choice</a>, with pigs often awarded to the winners of street games. Young men might <a href="https://brill.com/display/book/9789004251830/B9789004251830_014.xml">wrestle a greased-up pig</a> inside the Naples Cathedral, with the victor cooking the animal for supper.</p>

<h2>The road to cultural assimilation</h2>

<p>Centuries of devotion transformed San Gennaro into a symbol of Neapolitan identity. New York’s festival was designed to preserve those traditions.</p>

<p>That first Feast of San Gennaro in 1926 gave Italian immigrants a rare opportunity to publicly profess the cultural identity they had left behind in Italy.</p>

<p>It began with a procession featuring a 3-foot statue of San Gennaro. Hoisted upon men’s shoulders, the saint traveled around the church and the surrounding streets. While en route, <a href="https://www.instagram.com/p/DWmW_2njeUZ/">devotees tacked dollar bills to his body</a>, as many still do today. There was no blood relic, but there was a purported bone fragment of Gennaro’s specifically donated for the occasion. The chip of bone was placed in a circular container <a href="https://press.uchicago.edu/ucp/books/book/distributed/R/bo25041081.html">called a reliquary</a> and hung around the saint’s neck. Afterward, the Italians of Little Italy gathered around plates of roasted chicken to toast to their shared heritage and traditions. </p>

<p>The event was a big success. Just two years later, in 1928, <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/1928/09/23/archives/upsets-police-ban-on-parade-images-justice-callahan-finds-warren.html">The New York Times reported</a> that thousands of ex-Neapolitans were congregating for a festival that had already extended from one day to a full week. </p>

<p>But with triumph came trouble. That same year, New York Police Commissioner Joseph Warren prohibited the procession, arguing that the dollar bills pinned to the statue represented the “<a href="https://www.nytimes.com/1928/09/23/archives/upsets-police-ban-on-parade-images-justice-callahan-finds-warren.html">profanation of sacred religious symbols</a>.” The decision was ultimately reversed by a New York Supreme Court judge, on the grounds that Warren violated the populace’s religious liberties.</p>

<p>Warren’s attempt to suppress the procession exemplifies the sort of religious prejudices plaguing Italian communities during that period. But it was not the only form of discrimination Italians faced. </p>

<p>The darkness of southern Italians’ skin subjected them to discrimination, birthing <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2019/10/12/opinion/columbus-day-italian-american-racism.html">derogatory slurs</a> like “guinea” or “swarthy.” The suspicion that Italian immigrants were <a href="https://online.ucpress.edu/currenthistory/article-abstract/15/1/23/169598/Italy-s-Criminals-in-the-United-States?redirectedFrom=fulltext">prone to criminal behavior</a> was reinforced by real <a href="https://books.google.co.uk/books?id=2eCPAgAAQBAJ&amp;printsec=frontcover#v=onepage&amp;q&amp;f=false">mafia organizations</a>, such as the infamous Black Hand.</p>

<p>These prejudices, combined with the establishment of Italian churches and feasts, led to the belief that Italian immigrants clung too strongly to the traditions of their homeland and refused to assimilate into American culture. </p>

<h2>Non-Italians join the party</h2>

<p>It was not until after World War II that outsiders no longer hesitated to participate in Italian culture and festivities.</p>

<p><a href="https://www.nytimes.com/1949/09/19/archives/gay-little-italy-dances-in-street-fiesta-of-san-gennaro-draws.html">In 1949</a>, local newspapers reported that thousands of people of various ethnic backgrounds attended the riotous feast, where they watched Italians dance to folk songs in the streets and symphonic bands parade through the neighborhood beneath a new innovation: colored string lights casting pops of green, white and red along the city streets. <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/1956/09/11/archives/food-little-italy-feast-of-san-gennaro-provides-excuse-to-visit.html">Food played a big role</a>: Stalls piled high with fresh clams, pasta and pastries promised non-Italians an authentic taste of Italy. </p>

<p>From there, attendance ballooned. <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/1962/09/15/archives/little-italy-begins-san-gennaro-fete-buses-chartered-booths-open.html">In the 1960s</a>, chartered buses ushered in Italians from states as far away as Maine and Ohio. <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/1979/09/14/archives/san-gennaro-is-on-all-weekend.html">By the 1970s</a>, the feast had some 3 million visitors a year. Many locals today still recall how, in the 1960s and 1970s, young men <a href="https://www.dnainfo.com/new-york/20120917/little-italy/groups-want-revive-gambling-grease-pole-at-san-gennaro-fest/">climbed greased-up steel poles</a> set out in the street in hopes of claiming a cash prize. The oily affair was squashed over safety concerns in the 1980s.</p>

<p>Over the years, the feast has faced its <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/1996/01/02/nyregion/for-little-italy-group-famine-after-the-feast.html">own challenges</a> from within the Italian community. </p>

<p><a href="https://nypost.com/2011/02/28/san-gennaro-throws-no-dough-around/">In 2007</a>, some inhabitants of Little Italy petitioned Mayor Michael Bloomberg to cancel the festival, citing <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2002/03/17/nyregion/neighborhood-report-little-italy-mulberry-street-residents-grow-weary-living.html">the strain</a> that tourists placed on the local neighborhood and <a href="https://openroadmedia.com/ebook/the-italians-of-new-york/9781955835275">mafia interference</a>. In 1996, for example, <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/1996/06/12/nyregion/19-indicted-in-blow-to-genovese-mob.html">19 members of the Genovese crime family</a> were arrested for gambling, collecting dues from vendors and even stealing money off Gennaro’s statue.</p>

<p>Nevertheless, Bloomberg declined to interfere. The event, <a href="https://www.nydailynews.com/2007/03/28/san-gennaros-a-pizza-ny-says-bloomberg/">he said</a>, was a part of New York itself.</p>



<p>No one understands this more than the organizers of this year’s feast. When discussing <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LLJjTHly1BQ&amp;list=OLCvbfU0SOw0sci86fxt2mMpWhSgzn2Xw4A&amp;index=2">the plans for 2026</a>, the committee declared that this event was not just an Italian festival, but a tribute to New York’s cultural melting pot. </p>

<p>The 100th festival is dedicated to the Italian Americans who contributed to the city’s birth, an honor that arrives at a moment of controversy. Two months prior, Mayor Zohran Mamdani omitted Little Italy from a map of the city’s immigrant enclaves, <a href="https://abc7ny.com/post/mamdani-says-he-will-change-map-immigrant-neighborhoods-backlash-leaving-several-communities/19482161/">sparking immediate backlash</a>. While Mamdani vowed to reinsert the neighborhood, <a href="https://www.thenation.com/article/society/little-italy-mamdani-map-italian-immigration/">some argued</a> that the omission accurately reflected the <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2020/03/13/nyregion/arthur-avenue-bronx-little-italy.html">dwindling number</a> of Italians living along Mulberry Street.</p>

<p>The controversy underscores the question fueling the centenary: How should the immigrants who built the city of New York be honored, even as the descendants of many of those immigrants <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2018/02/19/nyregion/little-italy-manhattan-fire.html">have left their old neighborhoods</a> for different parts of the country?</p>

<p>Perhaps the answer is this year’s grand marshal, San Gennaro himself, who continues to serve as a bridge between the children of the Italian diaspora and their forefathers, just as he did in 1926.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/291237/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

Founded in 1926, the largest and longest-running Italian festival in the United States celebrates its 100th anniversary this year, with locals and tourists alike descending upon Mulberry Street in Manhattan to celebrate Italian American culture

To be sure, there’s plenty that’s commercialized: Frank Sinatra impersonators croon “New York, New York,” while vendors hawk shirts with quotes from “The Godfather” and “The Sopranos” at astronomical prices
Classic Italian American fare like chicken parm subs and sausage and peppers fly off food carts
And yet in my work as a medievalist , I’ve explored how this festival champions traditions that go back thousands of years
If anything, the fact that centuries-old rituals coexist with sweet Italian sausages and big, floppy pizza slices speaks to a lengthy, strenuous and beautiful process of cultural assimilation
From the Bay of Naples to Little Italy Between 1881 and 1920, over 4.5 million Italians immigrated to America
Thousands, most of whom hailed from southern Italy, settled on Manhattan’s Lower East Side to form what became Little Italy

These “ huddled masses ” faced all sorts of difficulties: overcrowded tenements, trouble finding work, racial discrimination and suspicion of their southern Italian Catholic practices , particularly from Irish Catholics
The Italian procession of religious statues and the street parties that followed, the Irish argued, looked far too pagan and idolatrous to be considered “real” Catholicism
Irish suspicion of such practices were also shared by local Protestants
But by the early 20th century, Italian communities had grown so large that they could fund their own Italian-speaking churches

Januarius, known in Italian as San Gennaro

He is also seen as something of a prophet

<title>Your robotic vacuum is a witness: What home robots mean for evidence, privacy and the law</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/760054/original/file-20260915-50-ap0vuz.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=93%2C0%2C893%2C595&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">The camera on a robot vacuum cleaner captured this cat. What else did it capture around the house?</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Portrait_of_Cat_by_Roomba.png"> voorts/Wikimedia Commons</a>, <a class="license" href="http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/">CC BY-SA</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>A husband in Taiwan suspected his wife of having an affair. In September 2023, he found a used toothbrush at their holiday home, and garage video showed an unfamiliar man driving his wife there. Three months later, he opened their robot vacuum’s app to speak with her and saw an intimate encounter through its live camera.</p>

<p>He recorded the feed and used it to win about US$16,000 from his wife and her lover for infringing on his marital rights. Then the <a href="https://www.scmp.com/news/people-culture/trending-china/article/3365381/taiwan-man-wins-lawsuit-gets-jailed-using-robot-vacuum-record-wifes-affair">Taoyuan District Court</a> sentenced him to five months in jail and fined him roughly $4,700 for recording private activity without consent.</p>

<p>Both rulings are defensible. Together, they expose a troubling gap: Devices in homes now generate evidence continuously and often invisibly, while the governing law remains a patchwork. As faculty members in a <a href="https://forensics.asu.edu/faculty/directory">school of interdisciplinary forensics</a>, we see such cases where forensic practice meets law that has not kept pace.</p>

<h2>The house that watches</h2>

<p>A modern robot vacuum is a mobile sensor platform. Some models combine <a href="https://us.roborock.com/products/roborock-s8-maxv-ultra-with-refill-drainage-system">cameras, microphones, laser navigation and remote video access</a>, while app-connected models create <a href="https://www.irobot.com/en_US/us-irobot-home-app.html">detailed floor maps</a> and cleaning histories. Their data may also reach manufacturers’ servers.</p>

<p>In 2022, <a href="https://www.technologyreview.com/2022/12/19/1065306/roomba-irobot-robot-vacuums-artificial-intelligence-training-data-privacy/">MIT Technology Review revealed images</a> from development versions of iRobot’s Roomba J7, including a woman on a toilet. Test-household images had gone to a data-labeling contractor, where workers posted them in private social media groups. No hacking was required; the leak arose from the ordinary pipeline used to train object-recognition software.</p>



<h2>Digital witnesses are already testifying</h2>

<p>Courts have confronted household data for years. Arkansas prosecutors charged James Bates with murder after a friend died in his hot tub, then <a href="https://www.nbcnews.com/tech/internet/prosecutors-get-warrant-amazon-echo-data-arkansas-murder-case-n700776">sought recordings from his Amazon Echo</a> and cited smart-meter data suggesting overnight water use. Amazon resisted until Bates consented. However, prosecutors could not eliminate other reasonable explanations, and they <a href="https://www.courthousenews.com/charges-dropped-in-amazon-echo-murder-case/">eventually dropped the charge</a>.</p>

<p>In Connecticut, Richard Dabate claimed that an intruder murdered his wife, Connie. Her Fitbit data contradicted his timeline and helped establish when she stopped moving. A jury convicted him, and in 2025, the <a href="https://law.justia.com/cases/connecticut/supreme-court/2025/sc20749.html">Connecticut Supreme Court upheld the conviction</a> and found the Fitbit evidence scientifically reliable.</p>

<p>In Ohio, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/1365712720930600">Ross Compton’s</a> pacemaker data was used to challenge his account of a house fire, raising a novel Fourth Amendment question: How much privacy protection should apply to intimate medical data generated by an implanted device? The court ultimately upheld the search warrant, finding probable cause and concluded that obtaining the data remotely was not an unreasonable search. <a href="https://www.journal-news.com/crime/prosecutor-man-awaiting-arson-trial-in-middletown-pacemaker-case-dies/article_a901f1f9-f661-5657-b688-347020d50a73.html">Compton died</a> before his arson trial date.</p>

<p>In short, household data can convict, exonerate or mislead. That makes digital forensics indispensable and demands careful guardrails.</p>

            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Three problems the law has not solved</h2>

<p>First is consent and notice. The wife in Taiwan argued that small indicator lights gave no meaningful warning, a concern that extends to guests, children, domestic workers and estranged spouses. Unlike a mounted security camera, a roaming appliance may record people who never saw its privacy policy.</p>

<p>Second, legality and admissibility do not always align. The constitutional exclusionary rule restrains government, not private parties, so the Fourth Amendment generally does not bar evidence wrongfully obtained by a private actor. The Supreme Court established that principle in <a href="https://supreme.justia.com/cases/federal/us/256/465/">Burdeau v. McDowell</a>in 1921.</p>

<p>How do the courts admit evidence potentially generated and extracted by private individuals? In the Taiwan case, what exactly was recorded? Where was it stored? Was it altered? These questions go beyond whether the video appears authentic; they determine what a court can reliably infer from a digital artifact whose chain of custody may begin with a participant in the dispute.</p>

<p>Congress created a different rule for aural communications. Under the <a href="https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?edition=prelim&amp;path=%2Fprelim%40title18%2Fpart1%2Fchapter119">federal Wiretap Act</a> of 1968, illegally intercepted wire or oral communications may be excluded, and the interceptor may face criminal and civil liability. When the act applies to recorded sound, illegality and inadmissibility can travel together.</p>

<p>Courts also disagreed for decades about one spouse recording another at home. The 5th Circuit created an interspousal exception in <a href="https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/appellate-courts/F2/490/803/122136/">Simpson v. Simpson</a> in 1974, but most circuits rejected it, including the 10th in <a href="https://openjurist.org/944/f2d/1537/heggy-v-tl-heggy">Heggy v. Heggy</a> in 1988. The 11th Circuit <a href="https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/appellate-courts/F3/347/1212/565284/">overruled its inherited exception</a> in 2003, leaving the Simpson ruling a conspicuous outlier.</p>

<p>A robot vacuum adds another twist: The Wiretap Act covers intercepted sound, <a href="https://openjurist.org/751/f2d/875/united-states-v-torres">not silent video</a>. Camera-only recording therefore falls outside that federal regime. Liability and admissibility then depend on <a href="https://www.rcfp.org/reporters-recording-guide/">state laws that differ sharply</a> in scope, consent requirements and penalties.</p>

<p>Third is reliability. Consumer devices were designed to clean floors, not withstand cross-examination; timestamps, firmware changes and retention policies can complicate interpretation. A remote-access log may identify an account without proving who used it.</p>

<p>Lawyers in the Dabate case challenged the Fitbit evidence on reliability grounds, although the court upheld its admission after expert review. Each new device category raises similar questions. Examiners need validated methods to acquire, authenticate and interpret data, as the <a href="https://www.swgde.org/">Scientific Working Group on Digital Evidence</a> <a href="https://www.swgde.org/documents/published-complete-listing/16-f-003-swgde-best-practices-for-the-acquisition-of-data-from-novel-digital-devices/">recommends for novel devices</a>.</p>

<h2>Charting a path forward</h2>

<p>Consumers would have a better idea of their exposure if manufacturers disclosed at the point of sale what a device records, where the data goes and how long it persists. Federal trade regulators already urge <a href="https://www.ftc.gov/system/files/documents/plain-language/913a_careful_connections.pdf">clear prepurchase disclosures and data minimization</a> for connected products. Those principles could be applied to remote viewing, not remain buried in terms of service agreements.</p>

<p>It would also help if manufacturers provided exportable logs showing when remote access occurred, which account connected and whether the camera or microphone was active. Federal <a href="https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-49/subtitle-B/chapter-V/part-563">vehicle event-data rules</a> offer a model by standardizing records and retrieval. <a href="https://pages.nist.gov/FederalProfile-8259A/technical/event/">Existing internet-connected device guidance</a> supports trustworthy time references, alteration protections, access controls and defined retention.</p>

<p>Legislatures could address intimate surveillance directly to prevent the current patchwork of laws from punishing betrayed spouses, enabling abusers and guiding neither clearly. Funding agencies and standards bodies could prioritize consumer-device forensics so that courts admit evidence because it is validated, not merely because it looks precise.</p>

<p>The vacuum in Taiwan did, in support of its primary function, exactly what it was designed to do: watch a room and report to the person holding the phone. The family and courts then improvised around evidentiary power that nobody had planned for. Congress and the states will need to decide what home robots may record, who may use the recordings and what they prove before words and actions in more homes end up as evidence in court.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/291849/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<title>At an old steel site in Pittsburgh, bacteria evolved to survive – and eat – industrial pollution</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/757604/original/file-20260902-60-j7pkeg.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C1%2C8256%2C5503&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">The author works on gathering soil samples in a field near Mill 19 in Hazelwood.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://cmu.widencollective.com/portals/zve7zami/UCM260305B_WTM_Armbruster#c3d884fc-5aec-4050-a605-3dc23a034272">Kevin Lorenzi/Mellon College of Science via Carnegie Mellon University</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Across Appalachia and the Rust Belt region, including throughout the city of <a href="https://theconversation.com/us/pittsburgh-news">Pittsburgh</a>, <a href="https://www.ura.org/pages/brownfield-projects">former industrial sites</a> are being transformed into <a href="https://www.ura.org/pages/southside-works">new neighborhoods</a>, <a href="https://19january2021snapshot.epa.gov/brownfields/brownfields-success-story-lawrencevilles-foundry_.html">research centers</a> and <a href="https://ridc.org/community-history/pittsburgh-technology-center-community-and-history/">technology hubs</a>. </p>

<p>But another transformation has been taking place beneath them for decades.</p>

<p>Brownfields are former industrial or commercial sites. Redevelopment there can be complicated by pollution. They’re often defined by what was left behind: abandoned factories, vacant land, and soil contaminated with carcinogenic compounds. </p>

<p>But beneath the surface, brownfields remain living ecosystems. Billions of microbes inhabit these soils. In Pittsburgh, some have spent decades responding and adapting to the pollution of the city’s industrial past.</p>

<p><a href="https://www.cmu.edu/bio/people/faculty/armbruster.html">I am a microbiologist</a> who became interested in this topic through a brownfield practically in my own backyard. My lab at Carnegie Mellon University is just 2 miles from <a href="https://hazelwoodgreen.com/">Hazelwood Green</a>, a 178-acre former industrial site at Pittsburgh’s riverfront along the Monongahela River. </p>

<p>For more than a century, this area was home to <a href="https://riversofsteel.com/">steelmaking operations</a>, including the <a href="https://www.pittsburghbeautiful.com/2024/02/12/j-l-steel/">Jones &amp; Laughlin Steel Co.</a>. At its peak, the site employed thousands of workers and helped earn Pittsburgh its reputation as the Steel City.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/757609/original/file-20260902-50-sgfgto.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Steel workers stand next to a trip hammer in a steel mill in a black-and-white photo." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/757609/original/file-20260902-50-sgfgto.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/757609/original/file-20260902-50-sgfgto.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=672&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757609/original/file-20260902-50-sgfgto.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=672&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757609/original/file-20260902-50-sgfgto.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=672&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757609/original/file-20260902-50-sgfgto.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=845&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757609/original/file-20260902-50-sgfgto.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=845&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757609/original/file-20260902-50-sgfgto.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=845&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Pittsburgh’s steel mills and coal-fired furnaces powered the U.S. through the 19th and 20th centuries, creating air and water pollution that remains part of the region’s environmental legacy today.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/steel-workers-stand-next-to-the-trip-hammer-in-a-steel-mill-news-photo/615294332?adppopup=true">Corbis Historical via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Pittsburgh’s industrial history also left a chemical legacy. Like many former industrial sites, Hazelwood Green contained soil contaminated with petroleum hydrocarbons, heavy metals and other pollutants, resulting in its <a href="https://benedum.org/hazelwood-green-transforming-a-brownfield/">classification as a brownfield</a>. Among these contaminants are benzene, toluene, ethylbenzene and xylene, a group of petroleum-derived compounds collectively known as <a href="https://www.atsdr.cdc.gov/interaction-profiles/about/benzene-toluene-ethylbenzene-and-xylenes-btex.html">BTEX</a>. These chemicals can be toxic to humans and other organisms, and some are known carcinogens.</p>

<p>Over the past several decades, substantial effort has gone into redeveloping Hazelwood Green. The remediated Hazelwood Green site is now a new center for research, technology and community engagement. This work, including remediating the site’s contaminated soil, raises an interesting biological question: What happened to the microorganisms that lived in these soils while they were contaminated? And can we learn anything from how they dealt with it to improve our ability to clean up other brownfields in the future?</p>

<h2>Pollution as an evolutionary experiment</h2>

<p>Soil contains an extraordinary <a href="https://www.globalsoilbiodiversity.org/blog-beneath-our-feet/2023/10/11/soilmostdiverse">diversity of microorganisms</a>. A single gram can contain billions of bacterial cells belonging to thousands of different species. </p>

<p>When pollutants like BTEX enter that environment, microbes encounter a new ecological challenge. For many organisms, the pollutant may be toxic. Some microbes, though, may already have metabolic pathways that let them tolerate the pollutant – or even consume it as food. That gives them an advantage over other bacteria at the same site.</p>

<p>Over time, pollution puts pressure on these microbes to adapt. Bacteria that can survive it — or even break it down — grow more common. And they can pass that ability to other bacteria, not just to their own offspring, by sharing genes directly. </p>

<p>At Hazelwood Green, decades of industrial pollution accidentally ran a giant evolution experiment for us.</p>

<p>My laboratory at <a href="https://www.cmu.edu/bio/">Carnegie Mellon University’s Department of Biological Sciences</a> wants to understand the results of that natural experiment. We are collecting soil from areas of Hazelwood Green with different historical levels of contamination. </p>

<p>Soil cores – cylindrical samples of soil drilled straight down from the surface, preserving its layers at different depths – allow us to examine microbial communities deep below the surface. We extract DNA from these samples and use metagenomic sequencing – a technique that identifies all the microorganisms in an environmental sample directly from its DNA, rather than growing and studying one organism at a time.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/757610/original/file-20260902-50-xnkl6v.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Four people work in an open field with scientific samples." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/757610/original/file-20260902-50-xnkl6v.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/757610/original/file-20260902-50-xnkl6v.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757610/original/file-20260902-50-xnkl6v.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757610/original/file-20260902-50-xnkl6v.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757610/original/file-20260902-50-xnkl6v.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757610/original/file-20260902-50-xnkl6v.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757610/original/file-20260902-50-xnkl6v.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">From left, first-year student Charlie Stanczek, lab manager Mara Kessler, professor Catherine Armbruster and second-year Ph.D. student Betsy Lewis work on soil samples.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://cmu.widencollective.com/portals/zve7zami/UCM260305B_WTM_Armbruster#7a3cdec5-35d4-460e-8a5f-9a91c30cedc5">Kevin Lorenzi/Mellon College of Science, Carnegie Mellon University</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Besides identifying which microbes are present, we want to know what they can do. One goal is to identify bacterial genes associated with degradation of BTEX and other hydrocarbons. </p>

<p>We’ve mapped decades of historical contamination records against the modern site, then compared microbial abundance across locations and depths to see whether past pollution left a lasting signature in these communities within Hazelwood Green. </p>

<h2>Finding microbes that eat pollutants</h2>

<p>DNA sequencing helps us understand what microbes might be capable of. But we also test those predictions directly. We isolate bacteria from Hazelwood Green and other Pittsburgh sites, then see whether they can use individual pollutants as food.</p>

<p>The basic experiment – a screen for BTEX-degrading bacteria – is simple. Normally, bacteria are grown in the lab in nutrient-rich media containing sugars, amino acids and other compounds they can readily consume. Instead, we grow them in a minimal medium where we leave out any carbon sources. Most bacteria need a source of organic carbon, essentially their “food,” to grow. </p>

<p>So we add a pollutant – benzene, toluene, ethylbenzene or xylene – as the sole carbon source in the media. If the bacteria grow, that suggests they can use the pollutant as food. In doing so, they remove it from the environment and help clean up the soil.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/757611/original/file-20260902-50-av2hbx.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A scientist scans a soil sample with a digital tool." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/757611/original/file-20260902-50-av2hbx.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/757611/original/file-20260902-50-av2hbx.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757611/original/file-20260902-50-av2hbx.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757611/original/file-20260902-50-av2hbx.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757611/original/file-20260902-50-av2hbx.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757611/original/file-20260902-50-av2hbx.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757611/original/file-20260902-50-av2hbx.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Catherine Armbruster, left, measures the levels of gases released by the soil’s chemical pollutants.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://cmu.widencollective.com/portals/zve7zami/UCM260305B_WTM_Armbruster#7a3cdec5-35d4-460e-8a5f-9a91c30cedc5">Kevin Lorenzi/Mellon College of Science via Carnegie Mellon University</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Finding those organisms one at a time is a slow process, so we’ve partnered with <a href="https://ai-science-foundry.cmu.edu/">CMU’s AI Science Foundry</a>, a robotic, automated lab located at <a href="https://www.gba.org/gba-project/bakery-square-nabisco-building/">Bakery Square</a>, another remediated Pittsburgh brownfield.</p>

<p>Robotic systems there let us screen thousands of individual species of bacteria at the same time and measure how well each one degrades pollutants such as BTEX. Meanwhile, open-source tools we’re developing, <a href="https://github.com/armbrusterlab/BTEXgenie">such as BTEXgenie</a>, search the bacterial genomes for genes that can help them degrade pollution.</p>

<p>This approach flips the usual order of discovery. Instead of studying one organism at a time and hoping it’s useful, we can scan thousands of genomes first to flag likely candidates – then confirm which ones actually work in the lab. Each round of testing also improves our ability to predict a microbe’s function from its DNA alone, so the process gets faster the more we learn. </p>

<h2>Can microbes clean up our pollution?</h2>

<p>Cleaning up contaminated soil is difficult and expensive. Common remediation methods – excavating contaminated soil or burying it beneath clean fill – can make land safe for redevelopment without actually eliminating the pollutants. This means long-term monitoring might be required afterward.</p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/Nj6cB6f0sow?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">In March 2026, the author’s team used a GeoProbe to collect soil samples up to 50 feet deep at Hazelwood Green.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Using microorganisms to remove environmental pollutants is not a new concept. Bioremediation is already used for <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/s13205-022-03199-y">oil spills and wastewater treatment</a>. In many cases, microbes naturally break down these contaminants as they grow, converting them into less harmful compounds. </p>

<p>However, bioremediation does not work equally well for every pollutant or at every contaminated site. One major challenge is identifying microbes that can degrade a particular contaminant while thriving under the environmental conditions where that contamination actually occurs. This is where studying microbes that already live in polluted environments gives us an advantage.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/757612/original/file-20260902-70-m98jnj.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A large machine is operated by a man wearing a neon yellow hat and vest." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/757612/original/file-20260902-70-m98jnj.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/757612/original/file-20260902-70-m98jnj.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757612/original/file-20260902-70-m98jnj.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757612/original/file-20260902-70-m98jnj.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757612/original/file-20260902-70-m98jnj.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757612/original/file-20260902-70-m98jnj.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/757612/original/file-20260902-70-m98jnj.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>

<p>By identifying these naturally adapted microbes – and figuring out how they metabolize pollutants – we may be able to improve existing approaches to bioremediation.</p>

<p>As former industrial sites across Pittsburgh and the Rust Belt become new hubs for science and technology, perhaps some of the biological innovations we need have been evolving beneath them all along. We’re only now beginning to discover what those microbes have learned.</p>
